new_statements.quote: REDUPLICATION: This is a common feature of Hmong occuring mainly in verbs and verbal adjectives. Have you noticed that when your informant says the reduplicated words at his normal rate of utterance the first word "loses its shape" i.e. the quality of the vowel is shortened or almost lost completely. There is stress on the second word. The contour of the tone is also changed - the first word having a shorter contour and the second word usually long and drawn out and on a higher pitch than the basic tone. [p. 37] ... The apostrophe (') used at the beginning of a syllable in pronunciation drills indicates the position of stress. [p. iv]
new_statements.citation: Whitelock, Doris. 1982 [1966-68]. White Hmong Language Lessons. Revised edition (Southeast Asian Refugee Studies Occasional Papers 2, series ed. Bruce T. Downing). Minneapolis: Center for Urban and Regional Affairs, University of Minnesota.
new_statements.locator: Lesson 3.C (Review), note 'REDUPLICATION', p. 37 (PDF p. 44); editor's foreword by Bruce T. Downing, p. iv (PDF p. 5)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (134 pp., text layer, UMN Conservancy scan, 'This report is not copyrighted'). extracted text of PDF p. 44 = printed p. 37 (page number '37' at foot) gives the REDUPLICATION note word for word as quoted, including the spelling 'occuring', 'There is stress on the second word', the tone-contour remark, the nasalization remark for 'ee'/'oo', and the drill items (koj tus nees loj loj li, koj tus dev me me li,...). PDF p. 5 = p. iv (Downing's 'A Note On This Edition', continuing from p. iii) has verbatim 'The apostrophe (') used at the beginning of a syllable in pronunciation drills indicates the position of stress.' A grep of the whole text for stress/accent/emphasis/prominence finds onl…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No word-stress rule is given: White Hmong words are monosyllabic and tonal, and the only stress statement is about reduplicated verbs/adjectives (loj loj 'very big', me me 'very small'), where the second copy carries the stress (longer, higher-pitched tone contour) and the first copy is reduced (vowel shortened, nasalization lost). The editor's stress apostrophe is used in the body only in English-based articulation drills.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; note that with nasalized vowels ee/oo the first (unstressed) copy loses its nasalization.
new_statements.domain_note: Reduplicative phrase (two-word expression) at normal speech rate; pedagogical description for learners, not a phonological analysis of the word. Language is monosyllabic and tonal (7 tones per the same source); no source opened states whether isolated monosyllables or compounds bear stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Whitelock's lessons represent White Hmong (Hmong Daw) as spoken in a mountain village in North Thailand, revised in Northern Laos (foreword p. iii) — the same variety as hmon1333. Niederer, Smalley, Golston & Yang and Garellek et al. also describe White Hmong (Thailand/Laos/US diaspora). The Lyman 1979 file is Green Mong / Mong Njua (different Glottolog languoid), included only as a related-variety check.

sources.locator: Lesson 3.C (Review), note 'REDUPLICATION', p. 37 (PDF p. 44); editor's foreword by Bruce T. Downing, p. iv (PDF p. 5)
sources.note: Editor's foreword (Downing) p. iv: 'The apostrophe (') used at the beginning of a syllable in pronunciation drills indicates the position of stress' (in the body the mark is used only in English-based articulation drills such as 'put.you, ap.'pa); Lesson 3.C p. 37, note on reduplication: first copy reduced, 'There is stress on the second word', with tone contour lengthened and raised on the second copy. No general word-stress rule.
